title: Excel vs Google Sheets: Which Should You Use in 2026?
dek: Choose Google Sheets for free, real-time collaboration and anywhere access. Choose Excel for heavy data, advanced analysis, and offline power. Most people are happy with Sheets; power users still need Excel. Here is the honest breakdown.

seo.metaTitle: Excel vs Google Sheets: Which Wins in 2026?
seo.metaDescription: Excel vs Google Sheets compared on price, collaboration, power, and offline use — with a clear recommendation for each type of user.

richText: Excel and Google Sheets do the same core job — rows, columns, and formulas — but they are built around different priorities. Excel is a powerhouse for analysis; Google Sheets is built for sharing and simplicity. The right choice depends on how you actually work, not on which is "better" overall. This guide breaks it down factor by factor, then tells you which one fits which kind of user.

body.richText: Google Sheets is free with any Google account, with no time limit and no feature paywall for the core spreadsheet. Excel comes with a paid Microsoft 365 subscription or a one-time Office purchase. There is a free Excel for the web, but it is a stripped-down version — the full power lives in the paid desktop app. For anyone counting costs, Sheets wins outright on price.

This is the clearest difference. In Sheets, several people edit the same file at once, changes save automatically, you see each other's cursors live, and version history is one click away. Excel has added co-authoring through OneDrive, but it is smoother and more reliable in Sheets. If your work involves other people touching the same file, Sheets removes a whole category of "which version is latest?" headaches.

body.text: Power and analysis: where Excel wins

richText: For serious data work — hundreds of thousands of rows, repeatable data cleaning, complex modeling — Excel is still ahead. Power Query automates importing and reshaping messy data, Power Pivot handles large data models, and the function library is deeper. Both apps do
, but Excel's charting and analysis tools go further. Finance, accounting, and analytics teams usually standardize on Excel for exactly this reason.

body.richText: Excel is a desktop app, so it works fully offline and stays fast on very large files. Google Sheets is cloud-first: offline mode exists but needs setup, and very large sheets can get sluggish because the work happens in your browser. If you routinely work on planes, in spotty connections, or with huge datasets, Excel is the safer choice.

items.question: Is Google Sheets as good as Excel?
items.answerRichText: For everyday spreadsheets and teamwork, yes — many users never hit its limits. For heavy analysis, very large datasets, or advanced tools like Power Query and Power Pivot, Excel is still more capable.

items.question: Can Google Sheets open Excel files?
items.answerRichText: Yes. Google Sheets can open and edit .xlsx files and export back to Excel format. Very complex Excel features — some macros or advanced formulas — may not carry over perfectly, so test important files.

items.question: Is Excel better than Google Sheets for large data?
items.answerRichText: Generally yes. Excel handles very large files faster because it runs on your computer, and it supports up to 1,048,576 rows per sheet. Google Sheets works in the browser and can slow down well before its 10-million-cell limit.

items.question: Do professionals use Excel or Google Sheets?
items.answerRichText: Both. Startups and collaborative teams lean toward Sheets, while finance, accounting, and data-heavy roles still standardize on Excel for its depth. Many professionals use whichever the task and the team demand.
